# Proof of the Binomial Theorem for Multiindices

Let $\alpha = (\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n)$ be a multiindex with $\alpha_j \ge 0$ for $j=1,\ldots,n$.
Let $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ and $y = (y_1, \dots, y_n)$ be ordered tuples of real numbers.

By the definition of multiindex exponentiation, we have:
$$(x + y)^\alpha = \prod_{j=1}^n (x_j + y_j)^{\alpha_j}$$

Since $x_j$ and $y_j$ are real numbers and $\alpha_j$ is a non-negative integer, we can apply the standard Binomial Theorem to each factor in the product:
$$(x_j + y_j)^{\alpha_j} = \sum_{\beta_j=0}^{\alpha_j} \binom{\alpha_j}{\beta_j} x_j^{\beta_j} y_j^{\alpha_j - \beta_j}$$

Substituting this into our product gives:
$$(x + y)^\alpha = \prod_{j=1}^n \left( \sum_{\beta_j=0}^{\alpha_j} \binom{\alpha_j}{\beta_j} x_j^{\beta_j} y_j^{\alpha_j - \beta_j} \right)$$

By expanding the product of these finite sums, we obtain a sum over all possible combinations of indices $\beta_j$ such that $0 \le \beta_j \le \alpha_j$ for each $j=1, \dots, n$. We can represent this sum over all such combinations as a sum over multiindices $\beta = (\beta_1, \dots, \beta_n)$ such that $0 \le \beta \le \alpha$:
$$(x + y)^\alpha = \sum_{0 \le \beta \le \alpha} \prod_{j=1}^n \left( \binom{\alpha_j}{\beta_j} x_j^{\beta_j} y_j^{\alpha_j - \beta_j} \right)$$

Using the commutativity and associativity of real number multiplication, we can rearrange the factors inside the product:
$$\prod_{j=1}^n \left( \binom{\alpha_j}{\beta_j} x_j^{\beta_j} y_j^{\alpha_j - \beta_j} \right) = \left( \prod_{j=1}^n \binom{\alpha_j}{\beta_j} \right) \left( \prod_{j=1}^n x_j^{\beta_j} \right) \left( \prod_{j=1}^n y_j^{\alpha_j - \beta_j} \right)$$

By the definition of the multiindex binomial coefficient and multiindex exponentiation, this equals:
$$\binom{\alpha}{\beta} x^\beta y^{\alpha - \beta}$$

Substituting this back into the sum yields:
$$(x + y)^\alpha = \sum_{0 \le \beta \le \alpha} \binom{\alpha}{\beta} x^\beta y^{\alpha - \beta}$$

This completes the proof.
